question: How much did the outcome change because of the intervention, beyond what changed anyway?

steps.title: Two groups
steps.text: Find a group that got the intervention and a similar one that did not. Unlike a trial, chance did not decide which was which.

quotes.text: The most important distinction is that treatment conditions are randomly assigned across units in an RCT but not in a DID design.

steps.title: Two periods
steps.text: Measure both groups before and after. Before, neither has the intervention; after, only one does.

quotes.text: In the first period, both groups are exposed to the control condition. In the second period, the treatment rolls out in group 2 but not in group 1.

steps.title: Change in each
steps.text: Take each group's change from before to after. The control group's change shows what time alone did.

quotes.text: RCT and DID share some characteristics: Both involve a well-defined study population and set of treatment conditions, where it is easy to distinguish between a treatment group and a control group and between pretreatment and post-treatment time periods.

steps.title: Subtract
steps.text: Subtract the control group's change from the treated group's change. What is left is the estimated effect.

quotes.text: DiD estimates the treatment effect by taking the difference between the change in the treated unit and the change in the control units in the periods before and after the intervention.

steps.title: Check the trends
steps.text: The method assumes both groups would have moved in parallel without the intervention. Plot several periods before it and see whether they did.

quotes.text: the time series of outcomes in each group should differ by a fixed amount in every period and should exhibit a common set of period-specific changes. Loosely speaking, a graph of the time series should look like a set of parallel lines.
researchers often plot the mean outcomes by group and time period and then ask whether the lines appear to be approximately parallel

exercise.title: Two subtractions, not one
exercise.intro: Ten years of an outcome in a treated and a control group; the policy starts in year 6. Compare a plain before-and-after reading with the difference in differences, then let the treated group drift upwards before the policy.
exercise.data_label: Example data, made up for this exercise with a fixed seed; the true effect is built in, so you can check each estimate against it.
